collate

kuh-LAYT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To collate is to collect and combine in order.

Before the meeting, the assistant had to collate the reports into a single organized packet.

Example

The clerk had to collate hundreds of loose survey pages before the results could be tallied.

Collate means to gather separate pieces of information or paper and arrange them into a single, properly ordered set -- a task often associated with paperwork or research.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

consolidate: To consolidate is to merge scattered things -- accounts, offices, piles of paper -- into one, with no promise about sequence. To collate is more exact: you bring separate pages or records together and also set them in their proper order.

organize: To organize is to arrange things into a clear, usable order, whether or not you had to collect them first. To collate bundles both steps into one word: round up the scattered pieces, then put them in proper sequence -- the classic word for assembling ordered paperwork.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

scatter: spread items out randomly

disperse: separate items widely

Where it sits · how much order gets imposed — gather → collate → systematize

gather vs. collate: To gather is just to pull papers into one pile, in no order at all; to collate goes further, arranging what you gathered into its proper sequence.

systematize vs. collate: To systematize goes further than to collate: collating puts one stack of pages in correct order, while systematizing builds a lasting, disciplined system for handling everything.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — col-

prefix — col-: together (Latin (variant of com-))

root — lat

root — lat: carried, brought (Latin (latus, past participle of ferre))

suffix — -e

suffix — -e: verb-forming ending (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: col- ("together") + lat ("carried") + -e (verb ending) = carried together -- gathered and combined into one set.

Use the root in a new word: translate

Use the root in a new word: translate: The same root gives us "translate," literally to "carry across" from one language into another.

Word Choice

Collate is an even-handed, mildly technical word -- it fits office or academic contexts naturally, though 'put together' or 'sort' would sound more casual in everyday speech.
